clue.text: Seat is adjusted for rest

indicators.note: something adjusted has been moved about and rearranged, so the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, doing double duty as fodder

explanation.surface: Someone tweaks a chair so they can lie back and take it easy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' works twice here: it joins 'Seat' to 'adjusted' in the surface and also supplies two letters to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A siesta is a short afternoon nap, a kind of rest taken in hot countries after lunch.

clue.text: Wine left outside home? Blow that!

definitions.note: a noun phrase: the thing you blow

indicators.note: something left outside sits around the edge, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: claret is red Bordeaux wine
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: Someone finds the wine has been left out on the doorstep and exclaims in annoyance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow that!' reads as a mild curse, but it is the definition: a thing you blow. 'left' is not L here; it means placed.
explanation.definitionFit: A clarinet is a woodwind instrument played by blowing across a single reed in the mouthpiece.

clue.text: Craftsperson who does not stand aloof from company?

definitions.text: who does not stand aloof from company
definitions.note: a relative clause describing a person

blocks.note: first meaning: a woodworker who fits timber together

blocks.clueFragment: who does not stand aloof from company
blocks.note: second meaning: a sociable person who readily signs up for clubs and groups

explanation.surface: A carpenter who likes to mingle rather than keep to themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word names a carpenter who makes joints and a person who likes to belong to societies; the question mark flags the playful second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes a woodworker fitting doors and frames, and also anyone keen on becoming a member of clubs.

clue.text: Beer that gives you wind

blocks.note: first meaning: beer drawn from a cask rather than bottled
second meaning: a current of cold air through a room

explanation.surface: A joke about a pint that leaves the drinker bloated and flatulent.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests gassy beer; the two senses are cask ale and a stream of air.
explanation.definitionFit: Draught beer is served from the barrel tap, and a draught is also a chilly breeze coming through a gap.

clue.text: Pit workers – children reportedly

indicators.note: what is reported is heard rather than read, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: minors are people under legal age

explanation.surface: A reminder of the days when youngsters were sent down the coal pits.
explanation.walkthrough: Minors, meaning people under eighteen, is pronounced the same as the coal-digging word.
explanation.definitionFit: Coal is dug from a pit, so those who labour underground there are colliery employees.

clue.text: Severe English author

blocks.note: stern means strict or severe
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A description of a strict, humourless English writer.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'Severe English' describe the author, but both words are wordplay and only 'author' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurence Sterne was an eighteenth-century novelist who wrote Tristram Shandy.

clue.text: William and directors providing a medium for advertisements

blocks.note: Bill is short for William
a company's directors form its board

explanation.surface: A man called William and a company's directors team up to run an advertising outlet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'William' leads to its familiar short form, and a group of directors is collectively a board.
explanation.definitionFit: A billboard is a large outdoor hoarding on which posters promoting products are displayed.

clue.text: See female awfully fit finally carry half a ton!

indicators.note: done awfully means done badly and out of shape, so the letters are jumbled
finally points to the very end of a word, so only its closing letter is kept

blocks.note: F is the standard abbreviation for female
taken as written, as fodder
the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: An onlooker marvels at a woman in terrible shape somehow managing to lift a huge weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is only an instruction to look at what follows. A ton is a hundred, both in cricket slang and in speed or money, so half of one is this number.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a ton is one hundred, so dividing it in two gives the number between forty-nine and fifty-one.

clue.text: Ace travelling to Saturn? One usually goes less far!

indicators.note: letters that are travelling are on the move and do not stay in their places

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for ace on playing cards
taken as written, as fodder

explanation.surface: A top pilot heads off to Saturn, though space travellers normally stay much closer to home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' looks like a link but belongs in the fodder. The definition is a wry one: space travellers have so far reached only the Moon, far short of Saturn.
explanation.definitionFit: Crewed spaceflight has never gone beyond the Moon, so a real space traveller always journeys a shorter distance than the ringed planet.

clue.text: Periods of world revolution!

blocks.note: surface reading: eras of political upheaval sweeping the globe
setter's reading: each time the Earth completes one orbit around the Sun, a fixed stretch of time passes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolution' suggests uprisings, but here it is the astronomical sense: the planet going once round the Sun.
explanation.definitionFit: Each complete orbit of the Earth about the Sun takes roughly 365 days, which is how the calendar unit is measured.

clue.text: German Mrs, a cheat for the most part

indicators.note: the most part is nearly all but not quite, so the tail end is cut off

blocks.note: a cheat or impostor

explanation.surface: A dig at some German married woman who is mostly a swindler.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the final D from the word for a cheat and the German title is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Frau is the German title placed before a married woman's surname, equivalent to the English honorific.

clue.text: Way grand house is mentioned

indicators.note: something mentioned is spoken aloud, so the word is judged by how it sounds

blocks.note: a manor is a large country house with its estate

explanation.surface: A road leading up to a stately home gets a passing reference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Way' reads as a road to the house, but it is the definition in the sense of a style or method.
explanation.definitionFit: A way of doing something is the style or method used, as in 'in a friendly fashion'.

clue.text: Troubled fool has rushed around

indicators.note: one thing placed around another encloses it on both sides

blocks.note: to hare is to run very fast, like a hare
an ass is a stupid person

explanation.surface: A worried idiot has been dashing about all over the place.
explanation.walkthrough: The fool is the one being surrounded: the running word goes around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone harassed is stressed and pestered by worries, which is what being troubled means.

clue.text: Woman to bring to trial?

blocks.note: first meaning: a common female first name
second meaning: to take legal action against someone

explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks which woman should face a court; the answer is both a girl's name and the verb for suing.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is a common female forename, and the verb means start a civil lawsuit against someone in court.

clue.text: Man and daughter getting on

blocks.note: D is the standard abbreviation for daughter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A father and his daughter get along well together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting on' looks like a phrase for liking each other, but only 'on' is used; 'getting' just attaches it.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is a common male forename, short for Donald, so it can stand for a fellow.

clue.text: Servant hugging old fellow on the river?

indicators.note: to hug is to wrap your arms around, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: a batman is an army officer's personal servant
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A manservant embraces an elderly gentleman while out on a punt.
explanation.walkthrough: A batman is the British Army term for an officer's orderly, not the superhero.
explanation.definitionFit: A boatman works on water, rowing or hiring out small craft, so he is a man found on a river.

clue.text: Man to bounce up and down

blocks.note: first meaning: a male name, short for Robert
second meaning: to move lightly up and down, as on water

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a bouncing man; the answer is a nickname for Robert and the verb for bobbing.
explanation.definitionFit: The short name is a familiar form of Robert, and the verb describes floating things rising and falling on waves.

clue.text: Woman offering article, newspaper's leader

indicators.note: the leader is the one at the front, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: an is the indefinite article
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A woman journalist pitches a piece to her paper's editor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'article' and 'leader' both sound like journalism, but one is grammar and the other just picks a first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ann is a common female forename, so any woman could be called by it in a crossword.

clue.text: Ruler wants stove to keep hot

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: an Aga is a brand of heavy cast-iron kitchen range cooker
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A monarch asks for a stove to keep the royal food warm.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aga is a British range cooker that stays on all day; H for hot comes from bathroom taps.
explanation.definitionFit: An agha was a commander or chief in the Ottoman Empire, a title for a man in authority.

clue.text: Flourish as British operator starting off

indicators.note: with its start off, a word loses its opening letter

blocks.note: B is the standard abbreviation for British
a surgeon operates on patients

explanation.surface: A British business owner does well as they launch their company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'operator' suggests a business or a phone company, but it is the doctor who performs operations.
explanation.definitionFit: To burgeon is to grow rapidly and thrive, just as a plant or business is said to flourish.

clue.text: Feeling of unease evident in German criminal

indicators.note: a thing evident in another is seen within it, so one piece sits inside

blocks.note: GER is the standard abbreviation for German
angst is a feeling of anxiety or dread

explanation.surface: An offender from Germany shows signs of nervousness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'German criminal' looks like one phrase, but 'German' is wordplay and 'criminal' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A gangster is a member of an organised gang of violent lawbreakers, so a crook.

clue.text: Firm's worker overseen by leading man

indicators.note: in a down clue, something overseen by another has the other placed above it

blocks.note: Adam was the first man in the Bible
a worker ant is the crossword's favourite worker

explanation.surface: A company employee is supervised by the chief executive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm's' reads as a company's, but it is 'Firm is': an adjective followed by the wordplay. 'leading man' is the first man, not an actor.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone adamant is unshakeable in their opinion and refuses to be persuaded, meaning resolute.

clue.text: Don't allow one outhouse to be got rid of

blocks.note: to ban is to forbid
I is the Roman numeral one
a shed is a small outbuilding

explanation.surface: Someone objects to having a garden outhouse demolished.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a past participle, matching the answer's form.
explanation.definitionFit: Banished means expelled or sent away, so something banished has been removed and dismissed.

clue.text: Fierce female in flower firm providing deliveries

blocks.note: first meaning: a warrior woman of Greek legend
extra hint: a flower is something that flows, a river, and this is the great South American one
second meaning: the online retailer that ships parcels

explanation.surface: A fierce woman working for a flower delivery company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' is a crossword trick: read it as flow-er, something that flows, so a river. The word is also a warrior woman and an online shop.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Amazons were a race of women warriors, and the same name belongs to the giant internet retailer.

clue.text: One cold summer in France with a cold drink

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral one, and C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
été is French for summer
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone spends a chilly French summer sipping a chilled beverage.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'cold' is wordplay for C; the second belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea served chilled over ice is a refreshing beverage served cool rather than hot.

clue.text: Ape going across an area at top of jungle?

indicators.note: to go across something is to span it from one side to the other, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: to ape is to imitate
taken as written

explanation.surface: A monkey swings across a clearing high up among the jungle treetops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ape' is a verb, meaning to mimic, not the animal; 'area' belongs to the definition, not the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: In a rainforest the canopy is the dense upper layer of leaves and branches formed by the tallest trees.

clue.text: Smart Conservative overcoming Left always

indicators.note: in a down clue, to come over something is to sit on top of it

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
L is the abbreviation for left
ever means always, as in 'for ever'

explanation.surface: A well-dressed Tory keeps defeating the political left at every election.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart' could mean well-dressed; here it means intelligent.
explanation.definitionFit: Smart and clever are synonyms describing someone quick-witted and intelligent.

clue.text: Animals having miserable sleep upside down

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning something upside down makes it read from the bottom up

blocks.note: sad means miserable
a nap is a short sleep

explanation.surface: Some creatures are having an unhappy, restless sleep while hanging the wrong way up.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole of the two joined pieces is turned over, not each one separately.
explanation.definitionFit: Pandas are black-and-white bears from China, so they are a kind of creature or beast.

clue.text: Produces notes maybe and runs a profitable business

blocks.note: first meaning, literal: prints banknotes, as a mint does
second meaning, figurative: earns a good income

explanation.surface: Someone composes music on the side while running a successful company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'notes' suggests music, but they are banknotes; 'maybe' flags coins as another possibility.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally printing currency and earning profits from trade are both described by the same common phrase.

clue.text: A link for G&S?

blocks.note: surface reading: some connection to Gilbert and Sullivan, the comic opera partnership
setter's reading: look at the symbol printed between the two letters, which joins them

explanation.walkthrough: Gilbert and Sullivan wrote comic operas together; the clue points at the typographical sign literally sitting between their initials.
explanation.definitionFit: The symbol & stands for 'and', so it is the character used to connect two words or letters.

clue.text: See 27
Trendy officer, usually

blocks.note: in means fashionable
a general is a senior army officer

explanation.surface: A fashionable military man, as he typically appears.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma splits the wordplay from the definition, which is an adverb phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean as a rule or in most cases, describing what normally happens.
